syllabus.clause: what atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability each actually promise

items.item: the 1983 coinage by Reuter and Härder, building on Jim Gray's earlier atomicity/consistency/durability naming

atomicity's own precise definition: all-or-nothing, in every situation including crashes
consistency's own engine-side definition: only valid-per-declared-rules state transitions

ACID is a 1983 coinage (Reuter & Härder) built on Jim Gray's earlier atomicity/consistency/durability naming; isolation was Reuter and Härder's own addition.
The real guarantees predate the acronym: IBM's IMS already supported ACID-equivalent transactions in 1973.
Atomicity means a transaction is indivisible: every statement succeeds, or none of their effects persist, even across a crash mid-transaction.

Consistency as an engine guarantee covers only what the schema actually declares: constraints, cascades, triggers. It says nothing about whether the transaction did what the application programmer actually meant.

The application owns the rest of 'correctness': any invariant not expressed as a declared constraint is invisible to the engine and can be silently violated by a transaction the engine happily commits.

Isolation is about concurrent transactions appearing as if they ran one at a time; the exact guarantee strength (which anomalies are and aren't allowed) varies by isolation level, from Read Committed up to Serializable.
PostgreSQL's own isolation mechanism is MVCC: each transaction sees a snapshot, not the live table, which is why Read Committed and Repeatable Read can see the identical interleaving differently.
Durability means a commit survives a crash; the real mechanism (write-ahead logging, already taught in §5.1) is what makes that promise physically true, not just contractually claimed.

A transaction's commit acknowledgment to the client is itself evidence the WAL record reached durable storage; a crash after that point must not lose the change, which is what distinguishes a real durability guarantee from an optimistic one.

ACID is a transaction-level contract; it says nothing by itself about distributed consistency across multiple nodes (a separate, later concern this chapter builds toward, not this refresher's own scope).

at.out: distributed transactions are out of scope for this refresher; named only as a boundary, not measured or taught here
